Visual Hierarchy

You might say

This page feels chaotic—everything is the same size. Layer it: headline dominant, description secondary, button most visible.

Visual hierarchy makes visitors read the page in your intended order—headline first, description next, button last.·Where the eye lands first on a page is not random: size, color, and position steer it. The headline is biggest and boldest so it lands first; the description sits one shade lighter so it reads second; the button carries a fill so it pops last. A page that "looks messy" usually has everything equally large and equally heavy, leaving the eye nowhere to start.
Know first
Typography
Same size versus layered

Four equal weights—nowhere to startThe test: squint—does the eye land where you want?
Three ways to layer

Size: More important means bigger. Headline clearly above subtitle, subtitle clearly above body—gaps wide enough to tell apart at a glance.

Shade and fill: Key content in dark ink, secondary one shade lighter; buttons stand out by fill rather than font size.

Position: Higher on the page gets seen sooner—things in the hero are noticed before anything at the bottom.

What it is not

Hierarchy is not typography—typography governs text size and weight, while hierarchy also covers color, position, and fill. It is not "content order" either: content follows reading logic, hierarchy decides how fast each block gets seen; they cooperate but differ. The diagnostic: squint at the page and check whether the first landing point is the one you wanted.
